chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar said: He informed me, Muhammad ibn Ismail from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Saeed al-A'raj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

He said: The Arabs did not cease to be upon something of the Hanifiyyah (uprightness/religion of Ibrahim), maintaining kinship, honoring the guest, and performing Hajj to the House. They would say, 'Fear the wealth of the orphan, for the wealth of the orphan is a shackle.' They refrained from certain prohibitions out of fear of punishment, and respite was not granted to them if they violated the prohibitions.

They would take from the bark of the trees of the Sanctuary and hang it on the necks of the camels, so no one would dare to take from those camels wherever they went, nor would anyone dare to hang something other than the bark of the trees of the Sanctuary. Whoever did that was punished.

And as for today, respite is granted to them. The people of Syria came and set up the catapult on Abu Qubays. So Allah sent upon them a cloud like the wing of a bird, which rained thunderbolts upon them, incinerating seventy men around the catapult.

key_terms.الْحَنِيفِيَّة: Uprightness or the pure monotheistic religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)

ai.seo_question: What were the characteristics of pre-Islamic Arab piety and how did divine punishment manifest in the story of the catapult?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (as) highlights that pre-Islamic Arabs retained elements of the pure monotheism of Ibrahim (as), such as kinship and hospitality, but lacked divine law (Sharia) and thus did not receive immediate punishment for sins. He contrasts this with the current era of 'imla' (divine respite), illustrating the concept with the historical event of the people of Syria who were struck by a thunderous cloud while besieging Mecca with a catapult on Mount Abu Qubays. This narration underscores the theological distinction between the pre-revelation era of natural monotheism and the post-revelation era of accountability.
